learningModules.title: Module 1: What We Measured vs. What We're Modeling
learningModules.description: What a public scan of your pricing page can and can't tell us, and the one number you should pull before changing anything.
learningModules.content:
What we measured directly: 4 plan tiers, an average of ~12 feature bullet points per plan (~48 discrete data points total), a 2.9s mobile LCP, and no usage-based cost estimator anywhere on the page. Those are facts about the page.

What we don't have: your actual visitor count, time-on-page, or checkout-initiation rate. Those live in your analytics, which we have no access to. Any specific dollar figure for unrealized revenue would require inventing a traffic number — we're not going to do that.

Hick's Law predicts that decision time increases with the number of options presented — at 4 plans, users face meaningfully more decision latency than a 2-plan architecture. Whether that's actually costing you conversions, and how much, is something only your own analytics can confirm.

How to check: pull your pricing_page_loaded → checkout_initiated conversion rate from whatever analytics you already have, before making any change described below. That single number is worth more than anything in this document.

learningModules.title: Module 2: Progressive Disclosure Architecture
learningModules.description: Redesign the plan selector to expose only the minimum information required for a confident decision, and reveal complexity progressively on demand.
learningModules.content:
The fix is sequencing, not simplification for its own sake — users can handle complexity if it arrives after commitment, not before.

Phase 1: Collapse from 4 to 2 visible plans (Starter and Growth). Gate Enterprise behind a 'Talk to Sales' CTA — but check your lead-source data first; if Enterprise self-serve is currently generating leads, don't remove that path, just de-emphasize it. For each visible plan, display exactly 5 features — the highest-value differentiators — with a 'See full comparison' expand toggle for users who want the rest.

Phase 2: Add a usage-based cost estimator above the plan cards. A single input (e.g. 'how many active users per month?') mapping to one recommended plan and cost. A 3-breakpoint slider mapped to your existing tiers is sufficient — it doesn't need to be a precise pricing model to convert value uncertainty into cost certainty.

We're not going to give you a specific expected lift beyond the modeled range in this document — that number only becomes real once you've measured your own baseline per Module 1.

learningModules.title: Module 3: PostHog Conversion Telemetry Setup
learningModules.description: Instrument your pricing page with the tracking events needed to measure the actual impact of each change and confirm or disprove this diagnosis.
learningModules.content:
Deploy these events in priority order:

1. posthog.capture('pricing_page_loaded') — baseline, fires on page load
2. posthog.capture('plan_card_hovered', { plan }) — reveals which plans attract attention
3. posthog.capture('plan_selected', { plan, price }) — critical conversion micro-step
4. posthog.capture('checkout_initiated', { plan, price }) — the moment of financial commitment
5. posthog.capture('estimator_interacted', { user_count }) — measures calculator engagement, once shipped
6. posthog.capture('pricing_abandoned', { time_on_page, last_plan_viewed }) — fires on exit intent

Build a funnel: pricing_page_loaded → plan_card_hovered → plan_selected → checkout_initiated. Your own conversion rate at each step — not the modeled range in this document — is what tells you where the actual drop-off is steepest. Check it weekly for the first 30 days after shipping any change.

learningModules.title: Module 4: Iteration Protocol — 30-Day Conversion Sprint
learningModules.description: The structured process to test, measure, and compound pricing page improvements over the first 30 days after the initial fix ships.
learningModules.content:
Week 1: Ship the 2-plan collapse. Measure checkout-initiation rate daily against your own pre-change baseline from Module 1. Don't make additional changes during this week — you need a clean data window to attribute any movement.

Week 2: Add the usage estimator. Measure estimator_interacted as a percentage of pricing_page_loaded. If it's low, the estimator likely isn't prominent enough.

Week 3: Analyze plan_card_hovered data. Heavy concentration on one plan with near-zero selection elsewhere may mean your tiers aren't differentiated enough, or a lower tier is priced too closely to a higher one.

Week 4: Review the full funnel against your Module 1 baseline. This is your actual, measured before/after — not the 10–22% range in this document, which was a starting hypothesis, not a target to hit.

diagnosis.signal: Acme Corp's pricing page displays 4 plan tiers with an average of ~12 feature bullet points each — ~48 discrete data points, measured directly from the page's HTML. The page also has no usage-based cost estimator and a 2.9s mobile LCP. We do not have your visitor count, time-on-page, or checkout-initiation rate — those require your own analytics, which we don't have access to. What we can say is that a page asking a first-time visitor to self-classify across 48 data points is a documented friction pattern; whether it's actually suppressing your conversion rate is something only your own funnel data can confirm.

friction.mechanism: Cognitive Overload — Choice Paralysis (measured structure, modeled behavioral impact)
friction.rootCause: 4 plans × ~12 feature bullet points require a first-time visitor to process ~48 discrete data points before committing to a plan. Hick's Law predicts elevated decision latency at this option count — a documented pattern in checkout-usability research, not something we've measured on your actual users.

finalDecision.label: Collapse pricing from 4 plans to 2 visible tiers
finalDecision.action: Redesign the selector to display only Starter and Growth by default. Reduce visible features per plan from ~12 to 5 key differentiators. Add a 'See full comparison' progressive toggle. Gate Enterprise behind a CTA only after confirming it isn't currently a working self-serve lead source.
finalDecision.reasoning: Of the three approaches, this is the one most directly grounded in what we actually measured — plan count and feature density — and the cheapest to ship and reverse if your own baseline data (Module 1) doesn't support the hypothesis.
finalDecision.tradeoff: Some power users may feel the visible feature list is insufficient; the progressive disclosure toggle addresses this. Skipping the Enterprise lead-source check risks cutting a channel that's already working.

decisions.label: Collapse pricing from 4 plans to 2 visible tiers
decisions.action: Redesign the selector to display only Starter and Growth. Gate Enterprise behind a high-contrast 'Talk to Sales' CTA once confirmed safe to do so. Reduce visible features per plan from ~12 to 5 key differentiators.
decisions.reasoning: Hick's Law predicts decision time increases with option count — moving from 4 to 2 plans directly reduces the measured complexity. Published research associates this pattern with higher checkout initiation, though that's a benchmark, not a measurement of Acme Corp specifically.
decisions.tradeoff: Some power users may feel the visible feature list is insufficient. The progressive disclosure toggle addresses this without cluttering the default view for the majority.

decisions.label: Replace the static plan grid with a single usage-based calculator
decisions.action: Eliminate the tier grid entirely. Replace with a single interactive calculator: one input, one recommended plan and cost as output.
decisions.reasoning: Removes the self-classification burden entirely rather than reducing it. Particularly effective for usage-based products where value is directly tied to scale — but a bigger, riskier build than option A with no more evidence behind the expected outcome.
decisions.tradeoff: Requires custom engineering for the calculator. The pricing model must translate cleanly to a usage formula, and enterprise edge cases may need a separate path.

decisions.label: Defer the pricing decision — activate a zero-friction trial gate
decisions.action: Remove the pricing page from the primary onboarding loop. Collect email only, grant immediate access, and present billing after demonstrated usage.
decisions.reasoning: Inverts the trust equation by moving the financial decision after value is shown, per general PLG activation research — but this is a bigger product and backend change than A or B, with the least direct connection to what we actually measured on the pricing page itself.
decisions.tradeoff: Delays subscription revenue per user and requires backend trial-gating work. If the core product experience requires live data to demonstrate value, the trial layer adds meaningful engineering scope.
